title: Memory Hierarchy in Practice
blurb: Tests memory coalescing and why access pattern beats data volume, array-of-structs against struct-of-arrays, shared-memory banks and the padding fix, when float4 and __restrict__ help and when they don't, register pressure, and what caching can't fix.

questions.prompt: When is a warp's global memory access coalesced?
options: When the data is already in the L2 cache
When consecutive threads read consecutive addresses
When every thread reads the same address at the same time
When each thread reads exactly one 128-byte line of its own
questions.explanation: 32 threads reading 32 consecutive 4-byte floats is 128 bytes, one burst, so the warp is served by one transaction. Caching helps reuse, but doesn't make a scattered pattern coalesced.

questions.prompt: copyStrided uses stride = 32 on 4-byte floats, so neighbouring threads are 128 bytes apart. With 128-byte transactions, how many transactions does one warp's read need?
questions.explanation: Each thread's float is in a different 128-byte line, so the warp needs 32 transactions for 128 useful bytes. A coalesced read needs one.

questions.prompt: In a 2-D kernel, which index keeps a warp's reads coalesced on a row-major array?
options: data[threadIdx.x * width + col], with threadIdx.x on the rows
data[threadIdx.x * threadIdx.x], so each thread reads a unique square
Any of these, since the L2 cache merges the reads afterwards
data[row * width + threadIdx.x], with threadIdx.x on the columns
questions.explanation: With threadIdx.x on columns, neighbouring threads read neighbouring addresses. With it on rows, they are width elements apart. The common mistake is choosing the CPU loop order without checking.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the L2 cache rescue a scattered, single-use access pattern?
options: Caches help reuse. Scattered reads still need fetching.
Scattered reads go straight to registers and skip the cache.
The L2 cache only stores data written by the host over PCIe.
The L2 cache is disabled for global memory reads in CUDA.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls this a common confusion. Caching pays off on reuse of the same data. A pattern that touches each line once, for 4 useful bytes, still pays for every line.

questions.prompt: Why does reading one field from an array of structs lose some coalescing?
options: Structs can't be stored in GPU global memory at all.
Struct fields are always stored in reverse order on the GPU.
Neighbouring reads are a struct apart, diluting each transaction.
The compiler converts each struct to a pointer, adding a lookup.
questions.explanation: Each thread's .x is 16 bytes from the next, not 4. A warp's request spans four times the bytes it needs, so only a quarter of each transaction is useful.

questions.prompt: A warp reads the .x field of 32 consecutive 16-byte Record structs. Across how many 128-byte transactions are those reads spread?
questions.explanation: 32 × 16 = 512 bytes span the warp's reads, which is 4 lines of 128 bytes. Only 128 of those 512 bytes are the .x values the kernel needs.

questions.prompt: AoS cost 2.55x SoA, while stride 32 cost 33.4x. Why is the AoS penalty smaller?
options: The strided kernel also has bank conflicts, which AoS avoids.
AoS reads go through shared memory automatically, which is faster than global memory.
Neighbouring AoS reads are 16 bytes apart, so a warp's request is only partly split.
The AoS kernel ran on fewer elements than the strided one.
questions.explanation: At 16 bytes apart, a warp touches 4 lines. At 128 bytes apart, it touches 32. Both kernels worked on 16.7 million elements, and neither uses shared memory.

questions.prompt: How many banks is shared memory divided into?
questions.explanation: 32 banks, one per warp lane, so ideally each thread in a warp hits a different bank in the same cycle.

refLinks.label: §40.2.2 Shared Memory Banks and Bank Conflicts

options: Threads reading shared memory before __syncthreads() has run
Two warps writing to the same global memory address at once
A block using more shared memory than its SM has
Threads in a warp hitting one bank at different addresses
questions.explanation: Different addresses in the same bank can't be served in one cycle, so the hardware serialises them. Running out of shared memory and missing syncs are different problems.

refLinks.label: §40.2.2 Shared Memory Banks and Bank Conflicts

questions.prompt: With the padded tile[32][33], element tile[r][c] is at word r × 33 + c, and its bank is that number mod 32. Which bank holds tile[5][3]?
questions.explanation: 5 × 33 + 3 = 168, and 168 mod 32 = 8. In general the bank is (r + c) mod 32, so reading down a column visits all 32 banks.

refLinks.label: §40.2.2 Shared Memory Banks and Bank Conflicts

questions.prompt: Why does reading a column of an unpadded tile[32][32] cause a 32-way conflict?
options: A column holds 33 elements, one more than there are banks.
Word r × 32 + c is always in bank c.
Each column read needs a __syncthreads() between the rows.
Columns are stored in global memory, so they skip the banks.
questions.explanation: (r × 32 + c) mod 32 = c for every r, so all 32 threads hit one bank. Padding to 33 makes it (r + c) mod 32, spreading the column across all banks.

refLinks.label: §40.2.2 Shared Memory Banks and Bank Conflicts

options: Forgetting to pad the matching global memory array as well as the shared tile itself
Padding the rows instead of the columns
Padding by 32 columns instead of 1, which doubles the tile's size
Padding every shared array by reflex, even those never read transposed or strided
questions.explanation: Padding costs shared memory, a limited resource that affects occupancy. Apply it where the access pattern causes conflicts, not everywhere.

questions.prompt: What does a float4 load do?
options: Reads one float four times, to check it for errors
Splits a float into four 8-bit parts for faster arithmetic
Loads four warps' worth of data in a single transaction
Moves 4 floats (16 bytes) in one instruction per thread
questions.explanation: float4 bundles four floats into one 16-byte instruction. It changes how many instructions a thread issues, not how many bytes a coalesced warp request covers.

refLinks.label: §40.2.3 Vectorized Loads and __restrict__: When the Bottleneck Is Already Bandwidth

questions.prompt: Why didn't float4 or __restrict__ speed up copyCoalesced?
options: float4 only works on fp16 data, and this kernel copies fp32.
__restrict__ slows down kernels that write to memory.
The compiler ignored both, because nvcc was run without -O3.
It already used full 128-byte transactions, with no aliasing doubt.
questions.explanation: The coalesced copy was already moving the most useful bytes per request, and in and out were used in the simplest way. The harness compiles with -O3. The chapter calls it a real null result.

refLinks.label: §40.2.3 Vectorized Loads and __restrict__: When the Bottleneck Is Already Bandwidth

questions.prompt: When does the chapter say float4 or __restrict__ is worth trying?
options: When the scalar version left transaction width or aliasing safety on the table
Never, since the null result shows they no longer work on modern GPUs
Only on compute-bound kernels, where memory access doesn't matter
On every kernel, since both are free wins that never slow anything down in practice
questions.explanation: Examples are kernels with complex indexing the compiler can't prove non-aliasing for, or kernels issuing many small sub-word loads. Treating them as free everywhere is the procedure's common mistake.

questions.prompt: How can unrolling loops and adding temporaries make a kernel slower?
options: Unrolled loops can't be compiled for compute capability 12.0.
Unrolling adds bank conflicts in shared memory.
More registers per thread means fewer threads fit on an SM, which lowers occupancy.
Temporaries are always stored in global memory, which is far slower than registers.
questions.explanation: Registers are a fixed per-SM pool. Spending more per thread trades occupancy for per-thread speed, and sometimes more is lost than gained. nvcc --ptxas-options=-v shows register use.

questions.prompt: copyCoalesced reads and writes 2^24 floats (4 bytes each) in 0.0715 ms. What is its effective bandwidth, counting both the read and the write? Give a whole number in GB/s.
Padding the transpose tile gave 1.15x. How does the chapter read that smaller-than-expected gain?
options: It shows the padding was applied wrongly, since conflicts always cost about 32x.
It's real. Conflict cost varies, so measure.
It is noise, since a 15% change can't be measured with CUDA events.
It means bank conflicts no longer exist on Blackwell-generation GPUs.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls it an honest finding, smaller than older documentation suggests for pre-Ampere GPUs. The correctness check confirmed the padded kernel transposes properly.

questions.prompt: A kernel reads a 2-D array with threadIdx.x on the rows and is 20x slower than expected. A teammate suggests float4 loads. What does the chapter suggest first?
options: Add __restrict__ to every pointer, since aliasing is the likely cause.
Put threadIdx.x on the columns to coalesce the reads.
Add float4 loads first, since they are the largest win in the chapter.
Increase the L2 cache size in the driver settings.
questions.explanation: With threadIdx.x on rows, neighbouring threads are width elements apart, the strided pattern that cost 33.4x. float4 and __restrict__ gave nothing on the coalesced kernel. The L2 size is fixed in hardware.

bookExercises.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain what makes a global memory access "coalesced," using the cache-line/burst idea from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: An access is coalesced when a warp's 32 threads request 32 consecutive addresses that fit within one (or a small number of) fixed-size memory bursts, commonly 128 bytes, so the hardware can satisfy the whole warp with a single memory transaction instead of many separate ones for the same amount of useful data.

bookExercises.prompt: Define a shared-memory bank conflict, and state the one-line fix this chapter uses to remove it in a tiled transpose.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A bank conflict occurs when two or more threads in the same warp access different addresses that happen to fall in the same one of shared memory's 32 physical banks, forcing those accesses to serialise instead of completing in parallel. This chapter's fix for the tiled-transpose case is a one-line change: declaring the shared-memory tile as `tile[32][33]` instead of `tile[32][32]`, adding one column of padding so each row's bank alignment shifts and the transposed access pattern no longer collides onto a single bank.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 40.1's table, classify each of the following as coalesced or not, and justify each in one sentence: (a) `data[threadIdx.x]`; (b) `data[threadIdx.x * 4]`; (c) `data[row * width + threadIdx.x]` with `threadIdx.x` indexing columns.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) `data[threadIdx.x]`: coalesced. Consecutive threads produce consecutive addresses directly. (b) `data[threadIdx.x * 4]`: not coalesced. Consecutive threads are 4 elements (16 bytes) apart, so a warp's 32 threads span a much wider address range than one burst, similar in spirit to Listing 40.1's `stride > 1` case. (c) `data[row * width + threadIdx.x]` with `threadIdx.x` on columns: coalesced. For a fixed `row`, consecutive `threadIdx.x` values produce consecutive addresses across the warp, the same pattern Listing 40.1's table marks as the coalesced 2D case.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter measured 1876 GB/s coalesced vs. 56 GB/s strided for the identical 16.7 million useful elements. Compute how many total bytes each version actually moved across the memory bus, assuming the strided version's scattered accesses each triggered a full 128-byte transaction for only 4 useful bytes.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Coalesced version: 16,777,216 elements, 4 bytes read + 4 bytes written per element = 8 bytes/element useful traffic, and since each warp's request is satisfied in one burst, total bytes actually moved is essentially the same as useful bytes: `16,777,216 * 8 ≈ 134.2 MB`. Strided version: the same 16,777,216 useful elements are touched, but if each scattered 4-byte access triggers its own full 128-byte transaction (for both the read and the write), total bytes actually moved is `16,777,216 * 128 * 2 ≈ 4.295 GB`, roughly 32x more physical traffic than the coalesced version for the identical useful data. That lines up closely with the measured ~33.4x effective-bandwidth slowdown (128/4 = 32, the stride used in the experiment).

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 40.3, explain in your own words why changing `tile[32][32]` to `tile[32][33]` removes the bank conflict, referring to how bank index is computed from a shared-memory address.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A shared-memory address's bank index is computed as `(address / 4 bytes) mod 32` for 4-byte data. With `tile[32][32]`, row `r`'s data starts at offset `r * 32` floats, so `(r * 32) mod 32 = 0` for every row. Every row starts on bank 0, meaning the transposed access `tile[threadIdx.x][threadIdx.y]` (which varies the row index across the warp) lands every thread on the same bank at a given step. With `tile[32][33]`, row `r` starts at offset `r * 33`, and `(r * 33) mod 32 = r mod 32`: a different bank for every row, so the same transposed access pattern now spreads across all 32 banks.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague claims "bank conflicts are basically as bad as uncoalesced global memory access, so always pad every shared-memory tile." Using this chapter's measured 33.4x vs. 1.15x results, write the two or three sentences you'd say back.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The two effects are not comparable in magnitude on this chapter's own measurements. Uncoalesced global memory access cost 33.4x here, while the unpadded bank conflict cost only about 1.15x, over an order of magnitude apart. Padding every shared-memory tile "just in case" is still low-risk since the fix is nearly free, but treating it as equally urgent to fixing a genuinely uncoalesced global-memory access pattern would be prioritising the wrong problem first. When time is limited, global memory access pattern should be checked before hunting for bank conflicts.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter measured a 2.55x AoS-versus-SoA slowdown for a 16-byte, 4-field struct, versus 33.4x for the stride-32 case. Using the "consecutive threads' addresses N bytes apart" framing from this chapter, explain why the two numbers differ so much even though both are coalescing losses.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The two numbers differ because the "distance between consecutive threads' addresses" differs by a factor of 32 between the two cases. In the AoS case, consecutive threads' `.x` fields are 16 bytes apart (one `Record`), so a warp's 32 threads span 512 bytes, roughly 4 memory bursts instead of 1, a partial coalescing loss. In the stride-32 case, consecutive threads' addresses are 128 bytes apart, so a warp's 32 threads span 4,096 bytes, up to 32 separate bursts instead of 1, a near-total coalescing loss. The AoS case still shares most of each burst's bytes across two or more threads; the stride-32 case shares almost none of it, which is why 2.55x and 33.4x are both real coalescing losses at very different severities.

bookExercises.prompt: Propose a kernel design (in a sentence or two, no code required) where fixing an uncoalesced access pattern would *not* meaningfully improve performance, and explain why, using this chapter's Trade-offs section.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A kernel that is compute-bound rather than memory-bound, for example one that does a long chain of transcendental-function evaluations (`sin`, `exp`, `log`) per element with comparatively little data movement, would see little benefit from fixing an uncoalesced access pattern, because the bottleneck is arithmetic throughput on the SMs, not the memory subsystem. Per this chapter's Trade-offs section, memory-access optimisations only pay off when memory, not compute, is what the kernel is actually waiting on.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the NVIDIA Developer Blog post "Using Shared Memory in CUDA C/C++." Summarise, in a few sentences, how its tiled-transpose example compares to this chapter's, and note any difference in the measured padding speedup it reports versus this chapter's 1.15x.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer expected. The NVIDIA blog's tiled-transpose example uses the same core pattern this chapter does: a `TILE x TILE` shared-memory tile, loaded coalesced and written back transposed, padded by one column to remove bank conflicts, and reports a real speedup from padding on the hardware it was measured on at the time. Because that measurement predates this book's Blackwell-generation reference rig, its reported multiplier is very unlikely to match this chapter's measured 1.15x exactly. The durable point, consistent across both sources, is that padding never hurts and typically helps by some modest amount, and the specific multiple is a function of GPU generation and cache/bank hardware, not a fixed constant to memorise.
